_comment: How an Arabic word on the page is turned into something the dictionary can be asked about. Read by lib/lookup.py; optional, like every file of this name. Arabic needs no `fold` -- the harakat come off with the language's own `strip` range, as they do for every language that has one -- but it writes its conjunctions, its one-letter prepositions and its object pronouns onto the word, and the dictionary lists none of those spellings: 5 of the 9 fixture verbs (فَرَأَى, فَقَفَزَ, وَذَهَبَ, وَقَالَ, أُرِيدُهُ) and 38 words of 30 of Wiktionary's own example sentences reached nothing.
_marbuta: A WORD IN -A WRITES ITS ة AS ت BEFORE A PRONOUN: قُوَّتِي is قُوَّة + -ī, and the plain -ī rule read it as قوت, food. These come first and put the ة back; where nothing is found that way (بيتي is بيت + -ī, and بية is no word) the plain rules below still answer.
_affixes: THE PRONOUN SUFFIXES and THE CLITIC PREFIXES, each written twice: vowelled, as a reading edition prints them, and bare, as a video's captions do. A vowelled rule is applied to the vowelled word and leaves a vowelled stem, which the dictionary's vowelled rows answer precisely -- قَالَ is `to say` and not the homograph `to nap`, which only the bare page title shares. Longest first, so that -hunna is -hunna and never -hu followed by nonsense. The article is not a rule: the tables list the definite forms, and wa- before one is one prefix.
